At narrow widths I would stack panels or offer an accessible tab layout. Toolbars should wrap or expose a compact menu. I would verify realistic long text, zoom and touch targets at several widths rather than only one desktop screenshot.
hints: Find the element that establishes the minimum width.
Some content needs local horizontal scrolling.
rubric: Uses responsive panel and toolbar behavior
Tests long content and multiple widths
mistakes: Hiding all overflow and making controls unreachable.
followUps: How would you preserve the editor's height?
When would tabs be better than stacked panes?
exercise: Create a two-column code/output layout and test 390px, 768px and desktop widths with a very long code line.

title: How do Angular signal, computed and effect differ?
lesson: A writable signal holds reactive state. A computed signal derives a value from dependencies. An effect synchronizes reactive reads with an imperative side effect.
example: Derive a cart total from cart items; persist a preference through a deliberately designed storage effect.
answer: I would keep source state in writable signals and use computed for values derived from that state. Angular tracks signal reads in reactive contexts so dependent work can update. I would reserve effects for appropriate synchronization with non-signal systems rather than copying one derived value into another signal. I would keep updates immutable where necessary and understand cleanup for resource-owning work. Signals do not remove the need to design ownership, asynchronous boundaries or component contracts. I would check behavior against the Angular version used by the project.
hints: Which value is the source of truth?
Derived state normally belongs in computed.
rubric: Distinguishes state, derivation and side effects
mistakes: Using effects as a chain of setters for derived totals.
followUps: How would you combine an Observable stream with component state?
Which effect would need cleanup?
exercise: Write a cart signal and computed total, then explain why no total-setting effect is necessary.

title: How would you explain Promise callbacks versus setTimeout ordering?
lesson: Synchronous code runs first. Promise reactions use the microtask queue, while timer callbacks run in later tasks when eligible; a zero delay is not an immediate execution guarantee.
example: Log A, schedule a zero-delay timer, schedule a resolved Promise callback, then log B.
answer: I would trace the synchronous stack first, then the queued work rather than guessing from the numerical timer delay. In the simple example, A and B print before the resolved Promise reaction, and the eligible timer runs later. I would clarify that real applications also have rendering, I/O and other queued work, so timing is not a performance guarantee. Long synchronous work and a stream of microtasks can delay responsiveness. I would test a small reproduction and keep platform-specific event-loop details separate.
hints: A delay of zero still schedules later work.
Trace the stack before the queues.
mistakes: Assuming setTimeout(fn, 0) interrupts the current function.
followUps: How can microtasks delay rendering?
Would Node-specific phases change the explanation?
exercise: Predict console order for A, B, a Promise callback and a timer, then run the sample.

title: When would you choose a controlled or uncontrolled form input?
lesson: A controlled input gets its current value from React state and reports edits through an event handler. An uncontrolled input keeps its current value in the DOM, which can be read when needed.
example: A search field needs live validation, while a simple upload form only needs its values when the user submits.
answer: I would decide who needs to own the current value. Controlled state is useful for live validation, dependent fields and reflecting changes elsewhere in the UI. For a simple form, an uncontrolled input with a default value and form submission may need less state. I would not switch an input between undefined and a controlled string after mounting. In either approach I would label fields, preserve user edits, handle reset deliberately and validate again at the server boundary. I would measure performance before optimizing away straightforward state.
hints: Who must react to each edit?
defaultValue is an initial value, not continuous control.
rubric: Includes accessible labels and server validation
mistakes: Assuming an uncontrolled field needs no validation.
followUps: How would a late network response avoid overwriting current edits?
How would you reset a file input?
exercise: Build a labelled search input with controlled state, then implement an uncontrolled version that reads FormData on submit. Compare when each value becomes available.

title: Why should rendering avoid mutating props or external state?
lesson: React may run rendering more than once or abandon work before committing it. A render calculation should derive UI from its inputs without changing data owned elsewhere.
example: A component sorts its props array in place, changing the order seen by a sibling even before the user clicks anything.
answer: I would keep rendering pure and create a new array before sorting or transforming shared input. An event handler can initiate an action, and an effect can synchronize a committed component with an external system when that is necessary. A ref can hold mutable information that does not drive rendering, but changing it is not a substitute for state updates. I would test with frozen inputs and development checks to catch accidental mutation. Repeated rendering should compute the same result from the same inputs without producing extra writes or subscriptions.
hints: Does the calculation modify data it did not create?
A repeated render should not repeat a side effect.
rubric: Derives output without mutating shared inputs
Places actions and synchronization at appropriate boundaries
mistakes: Disabling development checks to hide duplicate side effects.
followUps: Why can writing a ref during render still be unsafe?
Would useMemo make an impure calculation safe?
exercise: Write a pure helper that sorts products by price without mutating its input. Run it twice and verify that the original order remains unchanged.

title: Why do two Angular components receive different instances of one service?
lesson: Angular dependency injection resolves a token through an injector hierarchy. Providing a service at a component boundary can create an instance with a narrower lifetime than a root-provided service.
example: Two independent editors provide the same draft service locally so their current drafts do not overwrite each other.
answer: I would inspect where the token is provided, not only where it is injected. A root-provided service is commonly shared through the root environment, while a component provider can create a separate instance for that component subtree. I would choose the lifetime to match ownership and clean up subscriptions or resources when their scope ends. Shared state must be deliberate, especially when opening multiple editors. I would test identity and state isolation across sibling instances and avoid depending on a service being global when a local provider shadows it.
hints: Which injector owns this instance?
A component provider can shadow a broader provider.
rubric: Explains hierarchical resolution and provider scope
Tests isolation and cleanup between component instances
mistakes: Assuming every service is a singleton merely because it uses Injectable.
followUps: When would a shared cache belong in a broader scope?
How could a test accidentally use a different provider from production?
exercise: Create two independent counter panels with component-scoped services, then move the provider to a shared scope and describe how the behavior changes.

title: What should an Angular @for block track when a list can reorder?
lesson: A list's tracking expression describes the identity of each item across updates. Stable identity lets Angular associate DOM and component state with the same logical record after reordering.
example: A user edits the second row, then a new record is inserted at the top. Tracking the position can associate that edit with the wrong record.
answer: I would track a stable unique record ID for a dynamic list. An index may be appropriate for a genuinely static list, but not as a general identity for editable or reorderable records. I would ensure newly created unsaved rows also have stable local IDs and would not generate new random keys during rendering. Tests should insert, remove and reorder rows while checking focus and local field state. Tracking helps preserve identity; it does not replace validation or make duplicate record IDs acceptable.
hints: Is this the same position or the same record?
A key must remain stable across renders.
rubric: Handles unsaved rows without generating render-time keys
mistakes: Tracking array position for a list whose order changes.
followUps: What happens if the API returns duplicate IDs?
When would deliberately resetting a row component be useful?
exercise: Render an editable list using stable IDs and insert an item at the beginning. Verify that a draft and keyboard focus remain associated with the original record.

title: How can a discriminated union prevent impossible UI states?
lesson: A discriminant such as status lets TypeScript narrow a union to a specific state shape. This makes required data available only in states where it actually exists.
example: Separate loading, error and data booleans permit a screen that is simultaneously loading, failed and showing an unrelated success result.
answer: I would model distinct idle, loading, success and error variants with a literal status property. Success would require its data and error would require an error message. Rendering can switch on status and use an exhaustive check to catch a newly added variant at compile time. This improves internal correctness but does not validate data arriving from JSON; that boundary still needs runtime checks. I would test transitions and error rendering as user behavior, and avoid type assertions that bypass the guarantees the union is meant to provide.
hints: Which properties are valid only after success?
Compile-time narrowing does not parse an HTTP payload.
rubric: Models valid variants with a discriminant
Separates internal types from runtime validation
mistakes: Casting unvalidated network data to the desired union.
followUps: How would you represent refreshing while keeping old results visible?
What changes when a new cancelled state is introduced?
exercise: Define a request-state union and render every variant. Add a cancelled variant and use the compiler to locate handling that is no longer exhaustive.

title: How would you implement and test an array batching helper?
lesson: A batching helper splits an input into ordered groups without changing the input. Defining the size contract prevents zero or negative sizes from creating a loop that never progresses.
example: A list of five IDs with size two should become groups of two, two and one, while an empty list produces no groups.
answer: I would clarify whether the helper accepts only arrays and positive integer sizes, and whether groups contain the same item references. I would return new group arrays without mutating the original, reject invalid sizes and test empty input, size one, a partial final batch and a size larger than the input. The total work is linear in the number of items copied. For a stream too large to hold in memory, I would choose an iterator-based design instead of promising that batching an already-loaded array solves memory pressure.
hints: What happens when size is zero?
A new array does not necessarily deep-copy its items.
rubric: Defines size, order and mutation contracts
Tests empty, partial and invalid inputs
Explains linear copying and memory limits
mistakes: Using a non-positive increment in the batching loop.
followUps: How would you handle a lazy input stream?
Would mutating an object inside a returned batch affect the original object?
exercise: Implement batches without external dependencies and write edge-case assertions. Compare the original array before and after each test to verify preservation.

title: Search results sometimes show the previous query. How do you fix it?
lesson: Requests can complete in a different order from how they started. Debouncing reduces traffic but does not by itself make responses arrive in order.
example: A slow request for react returns after a faster request for react hooks and replaces the newer results.
answer: I would reproduce the race with controlled delays and ensure only the current request can commit results. I would use cancellation when supported and a request identity or ignore flag to guard stale responses. The guard must cover success, error and loading updates. I would represent empty, loading and failure states explicitly and clean up on unmount. A query library can manage much of this, but I would still understand its key and cancellation behavior. Debouncing is an optional traffic optimization, not the correctness mechanism.
hints: Which response is still allowed to update state?
A stale error can be as harmful as stale data.
mistakes: Only adding a debounce and assuming the race is fixed.
followUps: What if the transport cannot really cancel?
How would you test out-of-order failures?
exercise: Simulate two responses completing in reverse order and write the assertion that the newest query remains visible.

title: How would you design a multi-step form with conditional sections?
lesson: A complex form needs a clear state model, validation boundaries and rules for data that becomes irrelevant after an upstream choice changes.
example: Changing a sample matrix invalidates previously selected analysis rows in a laboratory form.
answer: I would model the form's domain data separately from the current step and define explicit transitions for dependent fields. Each step would validate what is needed to advance, while final submission would validate the complete payload on the server. I would decide whether hidden sections retain or clear values and test those rules. Draft restoration, back navigation and duplicate submission need deliberate behavior. I would keep the payload transformation centralized so the preview and submitted data do not disagree. Accessibility and clear field-level errors remain part of the design.
hints: What should changing an upstream choice invalidate?
The server must validate the complete payload.
mistakes: Keeping stale dependent IDs in a hidden section.
followUps: How would you version a saved draft after a schema change?
How would you keep preview and payload consistent?
exercise: Model one real multi-step form from your work. Write three transition tests for changing an earlier answer.

title: How would you choose local state, Context or a query cache?
lesson: Different state has different ownership and lifetimes. Server data, local interaction state and durable drafts should not automatically share one global store.
example: A filter popup is local UI state; shared user settings and cached API results have different invalidation rules.
answer: I would identify who reads and writes each value and how long it must live. I would keep transient interaction state near the component, lift state to the nearest shared owner and use Context for suitable cross-tree dependencies. Server data benefits from a query cache with keys, freshness and invalidation semantics. A reducer or external store can help complex client transitions, but I would not choose it simply because the app is large. I would avoid storing the same derived or server value in several independent places.
hints: Who owns the source of truth?
Ask how the value becomes stale.
rubric: Classifies UI, server and durable state
mistakes: Treating Context as an automatic replacement for server caching.
followUps: How would you reset state after signing out?
What belongs in a URL rather than a store?
exercise: Categorize the state in a ticket-search page and choose an owner and reset rule for each field.

title: A React page feels slow. What would you measure before adding memoization?
lesson: Rendering is only one source of latency. Network work, parsing, layout and excessive JavaScript can dominate a slow interaction.
example: A large filtered list triggers expensive calculation while an unrelated panel rerenders.
answer: I would define the slow interaction and profile a realistic reproduction. I would separate network time, main-thread work, React rendering and layout, then identify the expensive operation. I might move state closer to its owner, reduce unnecessary work, virtualize a long list or split code before adding memoization. If memoization addresses a measured bottleneck, I would check dependency stability and correctness. I would compare before and after on representative devices and avoid presenting a lower render count as proof of a faster user experience.
hints: Which user interaction is slow?
A rerender is not automatically expensive.
rubric: Validates an optimization with user-facing measurements
mistakes: Wrapping every component in memo without measuring.
followUps: When could memoization make things worse?
How would you avoid blocking while filtering?
exercise: Record an interaction timeline for a long list and propose one measured experiment.

title: How would you handle cancellable search in Angular with RxJS?
lesson: Observable composition can represent query changes and request lifecycles. Operator choice should match whether older work may be replaced or must finish.
example: A search box should show the latest query, while a payment submission must not be casually restarted or duplicated.
answer: I would normalize input, optionally debounce and remove repeated queries, then use switchMap for latest-query search behavior. Unsubscribing prevents the old inner stream from updating the subscriber, and Angular's HTTP integration can cancel the underlying request. I would place error handling so one failure does not permanently terminate future searches, and model loading and empty states. I would use framework-supported subscription cleanup. I would not reuse the same operator blindly for state-changing requests where every action needs delivery or duplicate protection.
hints: What should happen to an older search?
Where could catchError terminate the outer stream?
rubric: Matches operator semantics to the task
Handles errors without killing future searches
mistakes: Applying switchMap to every write request without considering side effects.
followUps: When would concatMap or exhaustMap be more suitable?
How would you test a stale loading state?
exercise: Draw the observable timeline for two rapid queries and one failed response. Describe the visible state at each point.

title: How would you choose CSR, SSR or static rendering for a page?
lesson: Rendering strategy depends on freshness, personalization, interaction and delivery constraints. A framework can mix strategies within one product.
example: A public tutorial, a live account dashboard and a marketing page have different caching and privacy needs.
answer: I would identify who needs the data, when it changes and whether the first response must contain useful HTML. Static rendering can fit reusable public content; request-time server rendering can support suitable dynamic needs; client rendering can fit highly interactive or browser-only work. I would discuss caching, hydration and error states rather than treating SSR as an automatic performance win. Personalized data needs strict cache boundaries. I would verify the relevant framework version and deployment behavior because rendering and caching configuration evolves.
hints: Separate public reusable data from personal data.
What must be visible in the initial response?
mistakes: Choosing one rendering strategy for every page without requirements.
followUps: How would stale public content be refreshed?
Why can an SSR page still have a slow interaction?
exercise: Classify a tutorial, account page and local-only code editor. Explain the trade-off for each.

title: Where should the Server/Client Component boundary go?
lesson: The client directive creates a module boundary for interactive code. It does not make exposed client values secret or mean every component should become client-rendered.
example: A server-fetched article contains an interactive bookmark button that only needs a small set of public props.
answer: I would keep data access and secret-bearing operations on the server, then introduce a narrow client boundary where state, effects or browser APIs are needed. I would pass serializable props and avoid importing server-only code into a client dependency graph. A Client Component can still participate in initial server-rendered HTML, so I would not define it as code that never runs on the server. I would inspect bundle size and verify authorization at every server mutation rather than relying on a hidden button.
hints: Follow the module dependency graph.
A hidden client control is not authorization.
rubric: Explains the client graph and initial rendering
mistakes: Adding use client to the root layout to fix one interactive button.
followUps: Can a Server Component be passed as children?
What would happen if a browser API runs during initial rendering?
exercise: Split an article with a bookmark control into a server data boundary and a small interactive component.

title: What tests would you write for a searchable editable list?
lesson: Valuable tests describe behavior and failure boundaries, not the exact arrangement of hooks or component internals.
example: A user searches, edits a record and receives a server validation error without losing their input.
answer: I would cover filtering, selecting the right record by stable ID, successful save and meaningful validation errors. I would simulate out-of-order requests, empty results and a failed save while checking that the user's draft survives. Unit tests can cover pure transformations; component tests can exercise accessible interactions; a small end-to-end path can check integration. I would avoid asserting private state or duplicating every implementation detail. I would prioritize risk and use a failing regression test when a real bug is fixed.
hints: What user data could be lost?
Which race needs controlled response ordering?
rubric: Chooses appropriate boundaries for each test
mistakes: Testing only that a button exists or a mocked callback was called.
followUps: What should remain real in an integration test?
How would you make a flaky race test deterministic?
exercise: Write a test plan with one transformation test, three interaction tests and one end-to-end scenario.

title: Why do CORS and a hidden API key not secure a backend?
lesson: CORS controls what browser scripts may read across origins; it is not general authentication. Anything shipped to a browser can be inspected by its user.
example: A frontend bundle includes a provider key, and an attacker calls the provider directly without using your UI.
answer: I would keep privileged keys on a trusted server and authenticate and authorize each protected operation. I would treat all incoming data as untrusted, validate it and apply suitable abuse controls. CORS can restrict browser-origin access but does not stop arbitrary HTTP clients. Cookie-based authentication also requires a deliberate CSRF strategy and secure cookie settings. I would avoid unsafe HTML rendering and review data exposure through responses and logs. The UI should reflect permissions, but the backend must enforce them independently.
hints: Could curl call the endpoint?
Can a user inspect the downloaded JavaScript?
rubric: Includes authorization and relevant browser threats
mistakes: Treating an allowed-origin check as user identity.
followUps: How would you protect a cookie-authenticated mutation?
What data could a verbose error leak?
exercise: Threat-model a public contact form and a signed-in project-save endpoint separately.

title: Tell me about a UI incident you owned.
lesson: An incident answer should show a causal explanation and a decision you actually made. Performance, accessibility and data-loss incidents all count when described accurately.
example: A conditional form retained obsolete IDs and submitted the wrong dependent choices.
answer: I would explain the affected workflow, how the issue was detected and my own responsibility. I would describe the evidence that narrowed the cause, the mitigation and the root change, then explain how I tested both the original case and nearby edge cases. I would state the result using evidence I actually have. If I do not have numeric business impact, I would not invent it. I would finish with a prevention measure such as a transition test, better validation or a safer release procedure.
hints: What changed your diagnosis?
Separate a visual symptom from the root cause.
mistakes: Saying only we fixed a bug without explaining how.
followUps: What alternative fix did you reject?
How would you catch it before users do?
exercise: Use a real project and write a five-part incident story with one supporting artifact for each technical claim.

title: When does a reducer make a multi-step UI easier to reason about?
lesson: A reducer expresses state transitions as a function of previous state and an action. It is useful when several fields must change together to preserve a business invariant.
example: A submission starts, clears an old error and locks editing. Success stores a receipt; failure restores an editable state with a message.
answer: I would list the valid UI states and events before choosing an implementation. A reducer can update related fields together and make impossible combinations easier to prevent. It should remain pure; network calls belong outside the reducer and dispatch results with enough identity to reject stale responses. I would test meaningful transitions, including duplicate clicks and late responses, rather than assert every internal field assignment. A reducer is not automatically better for a single independent toggle, and an overly generic action system can make a small component harder to understand.
hints: Which fields must change atomically?
A reducer calculates the next state; it does not send the request.
rubric: Keeps side effects outside the reducer
mistakes: Starting HTTP calls from inside the reducer.
followUps: How would you prevent an old request from completing a newer submission?
When is ordinary useState clearer?
exercise: Model idle, saving, success and error states for a save button. Add a request ID and show which completion events should be ignored.

title: Why did an error boundary fail to catch a rejected fetch?
lesson: Error boundaries contain certain rendering failures in a descendant tree. They are not a universal handler for every event callback, timer or asynchronous operation.
example: A component has a boundary around its results view, but a request rejected inside an onClick handler still needs explicit error handling.
answer: I would first identify where the exception occurs. A boundary can present a fallback for a descendant rendering failure, but an asynchronous request normally needs its own rejection handling and application error state. I would distinguish an expected API failure from a programming error, give users a useful recovery action and report safe diagnostic context. Boundaries should be placed around meaningful UI regions so one failure does not erase unrelated work. Reset behavior must clear the relevant failed state; an automatic retry loop can repeatedly trigger the same fault.
hints: Is the failure happening during render or in an asynchronous action?
Choose a recovery boundary that preserves unrelated work.
rubric: Describes the scope of error boundaries
Defines useful fallback, reset and safe reporting
mistakes: Wrapping the whole app once and assuming every exception is handled.
followUps: How would you retain an unsaved editor draft when preview rendering fails?
Which failures should users be allowed to retry?
exercise: Build a deliberately failing results component with a boundary, then reject an event-handler request and handle it separately. Explain the different recovery paths.

title: What makes an external-store subscription safe for React rendering?
lesson: An external store needs a subscription and a snapshot that changes identity when its data changes while remaining stable when nothing changes. A server snapshot must also support consistent initial hydration.
example: A getSnapshot function returns a new object every time, causing repeated updates even though the store value has not changed.
answer: I would use useSyncExternalStore for an actual external source rather than hand-build a render-time subscription. The subscription must return cleanup, and getSnapshot must return an immutable, cached value until the underlying data changes. I would avoid mutating a previously returned snapshot. For server rendering I would define a compatible server snapshot or keep the feature intentionally client-only. Tests should cover subscribe, unsubscribe, unchanged reads and changes between rendering and subscription. For state owned entirely by one component, regular React state is usually simpler than introducing a separate store.
hints: Are two unchanged snapshot reads referentially equal?
Can an old snapshot change after being returned?
rubric: Uses stable immutable snapshots and cleanup
Accounts for server and client initialization
Tests unchanged reads and subscription lifecycle
mistakes: Returning a fresh object from getSnapshot for every read.
followUps: How would you adapt a mutable third-party store?
Why might localStorage alone need an additional same-tab notification?
exercise: Implement a tiny immutable store with getSnapshot and subscribe. Verify that unchanged reads share identity and that unsubscribe stops future notifications.

title: How would you model a typed Angular form with a dynamic list of addresses?
lesson: A FormArray models a variable number of controls or groups. Typed reactive forms make the intended value structure explicit, while validation and nullable or disabled fields still require deliberate handling.
example: A checkout form lets users add and remove addresses and validates that the selected delivery address is complete.
answer: I would use a typed group for each address and a FormArray for the collection. I would define nullability, default values and validation at the appropriate control or group level. I would decide explicitly whether disabled controls belong in the submitted payload, since value and getRawValue have different purposes. Adding or removing a row must also update any selected-address reference safely. I would map server validation errors back to visible fields, retain entered values and test empty arrays, invalid rows, disabled controls and removal of the selected address.
hints: Which validation involves multiple controls?
Does the server need values from disabled controls?
rubric: Models dynamic typed groups with deliberate nullability
Handles group validation and submission mapping
Tests row removal, disabled values and server errors
mistakes: Assuming a TypeScript form type proves the submitted data is valid.
followUps: How would an async validator avoid acting on an outdated value?
What should happen to selection when an address is removed?
exercise: Build a typed address FormArray with add and remove actions. Write submission examples for an empty list, an invalid row and a disabled field.

title: What belongs in an Angular HTTP interceptor, and what should remain local?
lesson: An interceptor can handle cross-cutting request or response behavior. Request cloning, interceptor order and the destination of sensitive headers matter when centralizing that behavior.
example: An authentication interceptor must attach a token only to the application's trusted API, not every third-party request made by a feature.
answer: I would keep shared concerns such as approved API headers or request tracing in an interceptor and leave feature-specific validation and user messaging near the feature. I would clone immutable request objects when changing them, scope credentials to trusted destinations and understand the order of the interceptor chain. Automatic retries require an explicit policy for safe methods and idempotent mutations. I would test matching and non-matching URLs, existing headers, error propagation and cancellation. A centralized interceptor should not swallow failures or turn every response into a misleading success.
hints: Which destinations may receive this header?
Is replaying this request safe?
rubric: Scopes shared headers and clones requests correctly
Preserves errors and deliberate retry semantics
Tests chain behavior and third-party exclusions
mistakes: Attaching an application access token to all outgoing URLs.
followUps: How would concurrent unauthorized responses avoid repeated refresh attempts?
Where should a field-level validation message be handled?
exercise: Implement and test a trusted-API header interceptor. Include a third-party request that must receive no credential and a failing response that must reach the caller.

title: Why did subscribing twice trigger two HTTP requests in Angular?
lesson: HttpClient observables are cold: subscribing starts work. Sharing or caching can avoid repeated work, but requires decisions about subscribers, cancellation, invalidation and the lifetime of retained data.
example: Two view regions subscribe to the same unshared request observable and each starts a separate network request.
answer: I would confirm the subscription paths before changing the API. If the result should be shared, I would define the desired cache lifetime and choose explicit sharing behavior appropriate to the installed RxJS version. I would not assume shareReplay automatically creates a correct permanent cache. I would consider reference counting, errors, completion and invalidation after a mutation or account change. Tests should count requests and cover late subscribers, destroyed views and refetching after invalidation. For one consumer, removing an unnecessary second subscription may be clearer than adding caching machinery.
hints: How many subscriptions are active?
Sharing a request and retaining a result indefinitely are different policies.
rubric: Explains cold subscriptions and duplicate requests
Tests subscriber lifecycle and request counts
mistakes: Adding shareReplay everywhere without a logout or mutation invalidation policy.
followUps: When should a new subscriber trigger a new request?
How would you keep user-specific cached data from crossing account changes?
exercise: Use Angular HTTP testing to observe two subscriptions, then implement a documented sharing policy and verify both duplicate suppression and explicit invalidation.

title: Why can a Next.js page show a hydration mismatch only in production?
lesson: Hydration expects the initial client render to match the server-generated markup. Time, random values, browser-only storage, invalid nesting and environment differences can produce different initial trees.
example: A component formats the current time in the browser's locale while its server markup used another timezone.
answer: I would compare the first server and client outputs and identify the first nondeterministic value. I would pass a stable initial value from the server or intentionally render browser-dependent information after mounting, with reserved space where needed. I would check HTML nesting and extensions before blaming the framework. Suppressing the warning does not repair an incorrect tree, and making an entire page client-only can discard useful server rendering. I would reproduce the production configuration, locale and timezone and test both fresh navigation and direct loading.
hints: Which value differs before the first effect runs?
Server and browser clocks or locales may differ.
rubric: Uses deterministic initial data or deliberate client enhancement
Reproduces production and avoids blanket suppression
mistakes: Adding suppressHydrationWarning to every mismatched subtree.
followUps: How would you show a user's local date without moving surrounding content?
Why might direct loading fail while client navigation works?
exercise: Create a small time-dependent mismatch, then repair it with a deterministic initial label and an explicit browser enhancement. Test with different timezone settings.

title: How would you build a reliable save flow with a Next.js Server Action?
lesson: A server-side mutation remains a request boundary: its inputs, identity and ownership must be validated. Pending UI and cache updates must reflect what the server actually committed.
example: A user changes a project title, receives a validation failure and expects the edited title to remain available for correction.
answer: I would validate the submitted data and authenticate and authorize the specific mutation on the server. I would return structured expected errors, preserve editable values and show pending feedback without treating a disabled button as a security control. After a successful commit I would refresh the affected data using the cache behavior supported by the installed Next.js configuration. I would address duplicate submissions and failures independently of the happy path, and test that one user cannot modify another user's record. Unexpected errors would be logged safely and exposed as an appropriate recovery message.
hints: Who owns the record being changed?
A successful response must correspond to a committed mutation.
rubric: Validates and authorizes at the server boundary
Preserves input and accessible pending/error feedback
Updates affected data after a committed change
mistakes: Trusting a hidden owner ID or a disabled button as authorization.
followUps: How would you avoid a duplicate charge from a repeated submission?
Which failures should be returned as field errors?
exercise: Sketch a title-edit action and UI covering invalid input, unauthorized ownership, pending state and successful revalidation. Explain how you would test each branch.

title: Design a browser coding workspace for a large public audience.
lesson: Start with user journeys and trust boundaries before choosing libraries. Editing, execution, persistence and collaboration have different reliability and security requirements.
example: An anonymous visitor runs a snippet while a signed-in user saves a project owned by their account.
answer: I would clarify supported languages, file limits, execution model and persistence needs. I would separate editor state from execution workers or sandboxed previews, and keep untrusted code away from application secrets. Local drafts would work without an account; cloud saves would enforce server-side ownership. I would budget heavy runtime loading, mobile layout and cancellation, then add observability and abuse limits at remote boundaries. Collaboration would be a separate requirement with explicit conflict semantics. I would draw the smallest viable architecture first and identify what changes with scale.
hints: Which component handles untrusted execution?
Which state needs server persistence?
rubric: Covers loading, cancellation and growth trade-offs
mistakes: Designing collaboration and remote execution as ordinary React state.
followUps: How would you contain an infinite loop?
Which metrics identify a slow first run?
exercise: Draw the architecture of a real workspace you have used, then mark data ownership and execution boundaries.

title: How would you prevent an old tab overwriting a newer saved project?
lesson: Last-write-wins can silently lose work. Multi-tab and multi-device editing require a defined concurrency policy.
example: Two tabs load revision 7 and each attempts to save different edits.
answer: I would attach a revision or entity tag to the loaded record and make saves conditional on the version still matching. The backend would check and update atomically. A conflict would preserve the local draft and offer a reload, comparison or explicit merge rather than silently overwrite the newer record. I would distinguish this optimistic concurrency control from real-time collaborative editing. Offline work also needs durable local drafts, recovery and a clear synchronization status. Tests should force concurrent saves and verify ownership as well as version checks.
hints: Where must comparison and update happen atomically?
Do not delete the unsaved local version.
mistakes: Checking a revision in the browser before an unconditional server update.
followUps: How would you merge independent file edits?
How would deletion conflict with an offline edit?
exercise: Walk through both tabs saving revision 7 and write the exact expected result for each request.

title: How would you set and enforce a frontend performance budget?
lesson: A budget connects measurable user experience with engineering constraints. Lab tests and field measurements reveal different aspects of performance.
example: A page loads a code editor and a Python runtime before the visitor chooses either tool.
answer: I would identify important journeys and representative devices, then measure loading, responsiveness and layout stability. I would define budgets for critical JavaScript, heavy assets and key interaction timings, with both lab checks and suitable field signals. I would defer nonessential runtimes, split features and reserve space for late content. I would review regressions by user segment and set a release response when the budget is exceeded. One desktop benchmark or a high synthetic score is not sufficient evidence that every visitor has a fast experience.
hints: Which assets are essential before the first task?
Measure on realistic devices.
rubric: Defines user journeys and measurable budgets
Connects loading decisions to release controls
mistakes: Optimizing only a Lighthouse score while ignoring slow user interactions.
followUps: What would you do when third-party code exceeds the budget?
How would you diagnose layout shifts?
exercise: Audit one page and label each large dependency as critical now, needed later or unnecessary for the journey.

title: How would you introduce a design system without slowing every team?
lesson: A design system is a maintained contract for reusable behavior and appearance. Adoption, accessibility and change management matter as much as component count.
example: Several teams independently implement modals with inconsistent keyboard behavior and error styling.
answer: I would identify repeated high-value patterns and define accessible primitives with clear APIs and tokens. I would document composition, interaction states and supported variations, then pilot them in real workflows before demanding broad migration. Versioning and deprecation rules would protect consumers from breaking changes. I would test keyboard behavior and visual regressions where valuable, and measure adoption and duplicated work rather than the number of exported components. Governance should make useful contributions possible while preserving a coherent contract.
hints: Which repeated behavior is currently expensive or unsafe?
A component needs an adoption path.
rubric: Measures value rather than component count
mistakes: Building hundreds of abstractions before validating a real consumer.
followUps: How would you handle a product-specific exception?
Which change deserves a major version?
exercise: Design a modal API with keyboard behavior, focus restoration and one documented escape hatch.

title: How would you modernize an older Angular or React application?
lesson: A migration is a product-risk exercise, not only a dependency upgrade. Functional behavior and delivery continuity need explicit protection.
example: An older admin application has complex forms and weak automated coverage but must keep shipping changes.
answer: I would inventory dependencies, critical journeys and unsupported assumptions, then establish a small safety net around the highest-risk workflows. I would define a target and choose an incremental migration boundary where old and new code can coexist. I would separate framework upgrades from unrelated redesigns and track regressions and bundle impact. Each step needs a rollback path and clear ownership. I would challenge a full rewrite unless its benefits and risks are supported, and would confirm version-specific migration instructions from the framework documentation.
hints: What user workflow must survive every step?
Separate upgrade risk from redesign scope.
rubric: Inventories risk and protects core workflows
mistakes: Rewriting the whole application before verifying current behavior.
followUps: What would make a full rewrite justified?
How would you test compatibility across boundaries?
exercise: Create a three-step migration plan for a real form-heavy project, including a rollback signal for each step.

title: How would you avoid leaking personalized data through a server cache?
lesson: Cache reuse must align with data ownership and freshness. Rendering a page on the server does not automatically make every cache entry safe to share.
example: A dashboard response includes customer-specific prices and is mistakenly cached only by URL.
answer: I would classify data as public, tenant-specific or user-specific and inspect every caching layer, including framework data caches, response caches and CDNs. Personalization and authorization must be reflected in a safe key or the response must bypass shared caching. I would test two users and changing permissions, not only one successful request. I would also check current framework defaults and invalidation behavior for the exact version and deployment. Sensitive values should not be exposed through static output, logs or an accidentally public endpoint.
hints: Who may reuse this response?
A URL may not identify the current user.
rubric: Classifies ownership at each cache layer
Uses safe keys or avoids shared caching
mistakes: Assuming SSR disables shared caching automatically.
followUps: How would sign-out affect cached client data?
What would an integration test for a cache leak look like?
exercise: Trace two accounts requesting the same URL and mark every cache that must distinguish them.

title: How would you safely preview user-supplied HTML and JavaScript?
lesson: A code preview is an execution boundary. Escaping strings, sanitizing HTML and isolating code solve different problems and must match the feature's needs.
example: A playground snippet tries to read the parent page, navigate it or transmit data to an arbitrary host.
answer: I would choose a deliberately isolated origin or appropriately restricted sandboxed frame and verify its allowed capabilities. I would avoid combining privileges that undo isolation, restrict network and navigation where the product requires it, and validate the shape and origin of cross-window messages. Parent secrets would never be sent to the preview. I would handle infinite loops through an execution design that can be terminated where possible and enforce separate limits for remote code. I would test actual boundary escapes and never run untrusted code directly in the application's main context.
hints: Which capabilities does the preview truly need?
Messages are another untrusted input boundary.
rubric: Separates execution from parent secrets and resources
mistakes: Treating HTML escaping as complete JavaScript isolation.
followUps: How would you let a preview call a permitted demo API?
What can and cannot be stopped inside an iframe?
exercise: Threat-model a snippet that attempts parent access, navigation and an outbound request. Define a test for each.

title: A release increases frontend errors for a small group. How do you investigate?
lesson: Averages can hide a broken browser, locale, route or account segment. Observability must be useful without collecting unnecessary personal data.
example: A new editor works on desktop but fails on a mobile browser during runtime initialization.
answer: I would correlate the change with release versions and examine error rate by route, browser and relevant non-sensitive environment information. I would reproduce the affected journey, inspect network and initialization signals and compare with a known working version. I would consider a rollback or feature disable based on impact while the root cause is investigated. Logs would avoid source code and secrets unless deliberately consented to and protected. After fixing the issue I would add a targeted regression check and verify recovery in the affected segment.
hints: Which segment is hidden by the overall average?
Mitigation may come before a full diagnosis.
mistakes: Logging complete user projects to debug a startup failure.
followUps: How would you distinguish a provider outage from a browser regression?
What would trigger an automatic rollback?
exercise: Draft a minimal error report schema with diagnostic value and no source text, credentials or personal identifiers.

title: How do you handle disagreement about a technical design?
lesson: Senior judgement includes making assumptions explicit and learning from evidence. Authority alone is a weak substitute for a decision process.
example: One teammate wants a global state store while another proposes local state plus a query cache.
answer: I would clarify the user problem and constraints, ask each proposal to identify its benefits and failure modes, and separate reversible preferences from costly commitments. I would compare alternatives against agreed criteria and run a bounded experiment when uncertainty matters. I would document the decision, its owner and the conditions that would justify revisiting it. I would describe a real disagreement respectfully and explain what I learned, including cases where I changed my mind. I would avoid presenting disagreement as a contest I simply won.
hints: What evidence could change your position?
Which decision is reversible?
rubric: Communicates respectfully and records the decision
mistakes: Claiming seniority makes further discussion unnecessary.
followUps: What if the deadline prevents an experiment?
How would you support a decision you disagreed with?
exercise: Write a short decision record for one real disagreement, including the strongest argument against your preferred option.

title: Explain the hardest frontend system you personally delivered.
lesson: A senior project discussion should connect the user problem, architecture, ownership and results. Be explicit about work performed by other people or libraries.
example: A shipping-admin platform has conditional rules, overlapping schedules and several teams consuming its APIs.
answer: I would begin with the user workflow and the constraints that made the system difficult. I would trace the key state and API boundaries, explain my specific contribution and defend one important trade-off. I would describe a difficult bug or failure and the evidence used to fix it. I would give verified outcomes and acknowledge unmeasured areas instead of inventing percentages. Finally I would explain what I would improve with today's knowledge and how I would validate that improvement without disrupting existing users.
hints: Choose one deep decision instead of a feature list.
Separate your work from the team's work.
rubric: Defends architecture and a difficult trade-off
mistakes: Listing technologies without a request or state-flow explanation.
followUps: Which part would you simplify now?
What was the most important test you were missing?
exercise: Complete the project-defence worksheet for your own project and practise a two-minute architecture explanation.

title: How would you keep typing responsive while a large results view updates?
lesson: Transitions mark some state updates as non-urgent so urgent interaction can remain responsive. They do not move arbitrary JavaScript work to a background thread or make a synchronous loop cheaper.
example: A search field updates immediately, while rendering a large filtered result view can be interrupted and replaced by a newer query.
answer: I would profile the actual bottleneck and keep the controlled input update urgent. A transition or deferred value can let an expensive result render lag behind while I communicate pending state. If filtering itself blocks the main thread, I would reduce that work, index data or move suitable computation to a worker; merely wrapping the loop in a transition does not parallelize it. I would manage network cancellation and stale results independently. I would test fast typing, assistive technology and slow devices, ensuring the UI never presents old results as current without explanation.
hints: Separate input updates, computation, rendering and networking.
Priority is different from parallel execution.
rubric: Keeps urgent input responsive with explicit pending state
Targets the measured source of blocking
Handles stale data and accessible feedback
mistakes: Assuming startTransition moves every expensive calculation off the main thread.
followUps: Would list virtualization address a different part of the problem?
How would you measure whether interaction actually improved?
exercise: Profile a large searchable list. Compare rendering fewer items with marking result updates non-urgent, and document which part of the interaction each change improves.

title: What would you verify before moving an Angular application to zoneless rendering?
lesson: Zoneless rendering relies on supported notifications that tell Angular when views need checking. Code that depended on an implicit notification after any asynchronous callback may expose stale UI.
example: A third-party callback mutates a plain component field, but the view does not update because the integration does not notify Angular appropriately.
answer: I would check the installed Angular version and its documented zoneless configuration, then inventory asynchronous integrations, forms and third-party widgets. I would prefer supported mechanisms such as template-read signals, AsyncPipe and explicit change notifications at integration boundaries. I would test real user behavior and delayed callbacks without a test setup that accidentally hides missing notifications. Migration should be incremental with profiling and regression coverage, not a claim that removing Zone.js alone improves every workload. I would also confirm library compatibility and preserve accessible loading and error feedback.
hints: What actually notifies Angular that this value changed?
A test can mask a missing production notification.
rubric: Measures migration and tests stale-view failures
mistakes: Removing Zone.js and assuming all existing callbacks will refresh the view.
followUps: How would you diagnose a widget that updates only after a later click?
Which tests could give false confidence during migration?
exercise: Find one asynchronous integration and describe its view notification path. Test completion without another click or a manual test-only refresh.

title: How do you choose the scope and timing of cache invalidation after a mutation?
lesson: Cache behavior depends on the Next.js version and configuration. A useful policy distinguishes data shared by many pages from user-specific views and defines whether a writer needs immediate fresh data.
example: Editing a product should update its detail view and relevant listings without evicting every unrelated cached page or sharing a private draft.
answer: I would first identify which caches actually exist in the installed version, including whether Cache Components is enabled. I would map a mutation to affected data and routes and choose supported tag or path invalidation with deliberate freshness semantics. If the writer needs read-your-own-writes behavior, I would use an appropriate immediate-update mechanism rather than assume stale-while-revalidate guarantees it. Private data needs correct ownership and cache boundaries before invalidation is considered. Tests should include concurrent readers, related listings, failed mutations and deployment changes, with a fallback that avoids serving another user's data.
hints: Which readers need immediate freshness?
Do not mix examples from incompatible cache configurations.
rubric: Protects personalized data and tests concurrent readers
mistakes: Copying a cache recipe without checking Next.js version or configuration.
followUps: When is a path invalidation broader than necessary?
How would you test that a failed mutation leaves cached data consistent?
exercise: Draw the affected data for a product edit, a listing and a private draft. Specify freshness requirements and one verification case for each reader.

title: How would you catch a backend response change before it breaks the frontend?
lesson: A client mock can remain green while the actual API changes. Contract tests and runtime boundary validation connect assumptions in the UI to the payloads and errors the backend really provides.
example: A backend changes a paginated response from items to results, but a hand-written frontend fixture still uses the old shape.
answer: I would document the consumed request and response contract, including optional fields, nullability, pagination and error shapes. I would validate external data at runtime and test the consumer against representative provider responses or a verified schema in CI. Important integration tests should cover authentication failures, empty results and backward-compatible additions as well as success. I would avoid making every UI test depend on a live remote service, while ensuring mocks are checked against the contract instead of becoming an independent fiction. Rollout coordination and compatibility policy matter when clients cannot update atomically.
hints: Who verifies that the mock still represents the provider?
Additive fields and changed required fields have different compatibility risks.
rubric: Defines consumed success and error contracts
Combines boundary validation with focused integration coverage
mistakes: Treating a passing test against an outdated fixture as API compatibility proof.
followUps: How would you roll out a renamed required field safely?
Which contract checks belong in client CI versus provider CI?
exercise: Write a small response contract and three fixtures: valid, compatible extra field and missing required field. Describe the release gate that would reject the breaking provider change.

title: How would you paginate an editable table whose records change during browsing?
lesson: Stable cursor pagination needs a deterministic ordering and a tie-breaker, but its guarantees also depend on how concurrent inserts and updates affect that ordering.
example: Many records share the same created time; sorting only by that value can skip or repeat records across page boundaries.
answer: I would clarify whether browsing needs a consistent snapshot or may reflect live changes. I would define a stable total order, such as creation time plus unique ID, and have the server validate the cursor and authorization for every page. Updates that change sort keys require an explicit policy because a record can move between pages. On the client I would retain selection by record ID, handle deleted rows and avoid implying that the loaded page contains the entire dataset. Tests should cover tied keys, empty pages, concurrent changes and returning after an edit.
hints: Is the sort order total and deterministic?
A cursor alone does not create a snapshot.
rubric: Defines stable ordering and concurrency guarantees
Preserves record identity and server authorization
Tests tied keys, mutations and incomplete loaded data
mistakes: Assuming cursor pagination automatically prevents all skips during concurrent edits.
followUps: When would an immutable snapshot token be needed?
How should select-all work when only one page is loaded?
exercise: Design a cursor for records ordered by created time and ID. Walk through tied timestamps and an edit that moves a row, stating the user-visible policy.

title: How would you keep a real-time UI correct after duplicate or out-of-order events?
lesson: A transport delivering messages does not by itself define application ordering or recovery. Versioned records and a resynchronization protocol help the client identify stale events and missing state.
example: The UI receives version five of a record and then version four after reconnecting. Applying both in arrival order rolls the display backward.
answer: I would define event identity, record versioning and deletion semantics with the backend. The client would apply only valid newer updates and deduplicate repeats, while detecting gaps according to the actual protocol. Reconnection needs a supported resume cursor or an authoritative refetch rather than assuming a socket restores missed state automatically. Local optimistic edits need reconciliation with server-confirmed versions. I would test duplicated, reversed and missing events, account changes and expired resume tokens. Observability should reveal repeated resynchronization without exposing sensitive payloads in client logs.
hints: Does arrival order equal record version order?
A deleted record must not reappear from a late update.
rubric: Tests stale updates, deletion and optimistic conflicts
mistakes: Treating a reopened WebSocket as proof that missed events were recovered.
followUps: When should a version gap trigger a refetch?
How would a deletion tombstone prevent resurrection?
exercise: Write a pure version-merge helper and feed it repeated and reversed updates. Then specify which missing-event case requires authoritative resynchronization rather than guessing.
